subtype: Insults, taunts and challenges among peers [Interpreting]
passage: Noor, when I was fifteen, and yes, this is your Hafsa khala talking, a boy named Pran said, in front of the whole bus, "Nice haircut, did you lose a bet?" Everyone laughed. I didn't know if he was joking, because he said it with a grin and we had teased each other for years. I looked at my friends. They were laughing at him too, so I laughed and said, "Yes, I lost to a goat." That was banter. But a month later a boy from another school sent nasty messages in a group chat and dared me to answer, again and again. That felt like an attack meant to provoke. I did not answer. I took screenshots and showed my mother, and the messages stopped.

qa.q: Where did Pran make the remark about the haircut?
qa.a: He made it on the bus, in front of everyone.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa feel the messages from the boy from another school were different?
qa.a: They were nasty, repeated and came with dares to answer, so she felt wary and treated them as an attack meant to provoke. Pran's remark came with a grin from someone she had teased for years.

qa.q: What protective steps did Hafsa take?
qa.a: She did not answer, saved screenshots and showed her mother.

qa.q: How might Pran have seen his joke on the bus?
qa.a: Probably as ordinary teasing between friends, though it may not have felt the same to everyone listening.

grounding: An elder tells how tone, history and audience separate banter from attack, and not answering and saving evidence protect.

subtype: Insults, taunts and challenges among peers [Interpreting]
passage: The bus was loud and the match on the driver's radio drowned out most of it. Bhavna's phone buzzed. In the class group, a boy had posted, 'Bet you can't score even one goal, Bhavna. Dare you to try in front of everyone.' A few laughing emojis followed. Minakshi, sitting next to her, leaned over. "Is this a joke or a shove?" Bhavna's cheeks burned. She looked at who sent it, remembered he had done this before, and noticed the crowd of watchers. "It's not friendly." She did not type a reply. Instead she took a screenshot and whispered, "Can you help me show this to Ma'am tomorrow?" Minakshi nodded and squeezed her hand.

qa.q: Whose phone buzzed on the bus?
qa.a: Bhavna's phone buzzed.

qa.q: What made Bhavna decide the message was not friendly?
qa.a: She looked at who sent it, remembered he had done this before and noticed the crowd watching, so it felt like a shove meant to provoke her. Her burning cheeks show it hurt.

qa.q: What steps did Bhavna take that protect her?
qa.a: She did not reply, she took a screenshot and asked Minakshi to help show it to Ma'am.

qa.q: How might the boy who posted it see the message?
qa.a: He may say he was only joking, but the past pattern and the audience suggest it was meant to provoke.

grounding: A teen reads tone, history and audience to see an online taunt as an attack, and does not reply but saves evidence.

subtype: Insults, taunts and challenges among peers [Interpreting]
passage:
Aparna posted a thirty-second dance video on a Thursday night. By morning there were two comments that looked almost the same.
One was from Ganga, her friend since Class 3: "potato legs strike again 🥔😂". The other was from an account with no photo, created that week: "can't even move lol. delete this."
Aparna read them both at the breakfast table in their flat in Pune. Ganga's made her snort; they had called each other "potato" since they were eight. The other made her stomach tighten.
The second account had also commented on two other girls' videos from her school, each time with a laugh and "delete this." Plenty of people had liked those comments.
Aparna didn't reply. She took screenshots of all three, blocked the account, and showed her mother, who helped her report it. Then she replied to Ganga: "potato legs forever."

qa.q: How long was Aparna's dance video?
qa.a: It was a thirty-second dance video.

qa.q: Why did the two similar comments make Aparna feel so differently?
qa.a: Ganga's comment felt funny and warm because of their long history, while the stranger's made her anxious, since it came from a new account attacking several girls.

qa.q: What protective steps did Aparna take with the second comment?
qa.a: She didn't reply, saved screenshots, blocked the account and reported it with her mother's help.

qa.q: How might the other girls from her school have felt seeing those comments liked by many people?
qa.a: They probably felt hurt and exposed, and the likes may have made the attack feel bigger and more public.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager reading tone, history and audience to tell banter from an attack, and not answering while saving evidence.

subtype: Insults, taunts and challenges among peers [Interpreting]
passage:
"Oye, Lavanya! Bet you're too scared to answer Sir back tomorrow. Scaredy cat."
Laughter from the back of the bus.
Lavanya went red. "I'm not scared."
"Then prove it!"
Tanuja pulled her down into the seat. "Don't."
"But they're calling me scared."
"Listen to how they're saying it. They're not laughing with you. They want you to get in trouble in front of everyone."
"Karan's my friend, though."
"Karan joked about your pencil box last week and it was fine. This is different. Look, the whole back row is filming."
Lavanya looked. Two phones were pointed at her.
She turned to face the front. "I don't have to prove anything."
"Nope."
"Scaredy cat!" someone yelled again.
Lavanya didn't turn around. Tanuja said, "Good. Tomorrow, if they post anything, we save it and show Ma'am."

qa.q: What were two people in the back row doing?
qa.a: Two phones were pointed at Lavanya; the back row was filming.

qa.q: How was Lavanya feeling when she was called a scaredy cat?
qa.a: Lavanya felt embarrassed and provoked, her face going red, and wanted to prove she wasn't scared.

qa.q: How did Tanuja help Lavanya read the taunt?
qa.a: She pointed out the tone, the difference from Karan's usual jokes, and the filming audience, which showed it was meant to provoke rather than banter.

qa.q: What would change if Lavanya had taken the dare?
qa.a: She would likely have ended up in trouble in front of everyone, with the moment filmed and possibly shared.

grounding: The dialogue shows a teenager reading a taunt through tone, history and audience, and choosing not to answer.

subtype: Insults, taunts and challenges among peers [Interpreting]
passage:
In our cricket group chat, Harish has called me "Professor" since Class 6, because I'm always correcting scorecards. When he writes "Professor, what's the run rate?", I laugh and answer. That's us.
Last month a new number joined the group. Within a day it posted, "Vijay the Professor of losing 😂" and then, three times that week, "everyone hates you, just leave." Each time, a couple of people reacted with laughing faces.
It looked a bit like Harish's jokes, but it wasn't. No history, no smile behind it, and it wanted an audience to watch me fight back.
I didn't answer. I took screenshots of every message with the date and time. Harish did the same. That evening I showed my older brother, and he sat with me while we reported the number to the class teacher by email.
She removed it from the group the next morning.

qa.q: How long has Harish called Vijay "Professor"?
qa.a: Harish has called Vijay "Professor" since Class 6.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel about the new number's messages, compared with Harish's jokes?
qa.a: Vijay saw that the new messages had no shared history, carried hostility rather than a smile, and seemed aimed at an audience, which made Vijay feel wary and hurt rather than amused.

qa.q: Which of Vijay's steps were most protective?
qa.a: Not answering, saving screenshots with dates and times, and telling an older brother, who helped report it to the class teacher that evening.

qa.q: How might Harish see the difference between his joke and the new messages?
qa.a: Harish seems to see the new messages as an attack, since he saved screenshots too instead of joining in.

grounding: The account shows a teenager reading tone, history and audience to tell banter from a provocation, and not answering while saving evidence.

subtype: Insults, taunts and challenges among peers [Interpreting]
passage:
Tuition centre, teacher's note, Friday evening
Manjula stayed back after the maths batch, scrolling her phone with her lips pressed tight. She showed me two messages. One from Nazia, who sits beside her: "fail queen strikes again 😜 chai tomorrow?" The other from an account with no photo, under the class video: "everyone knows you cheated, loser, cry about it." Manjula said she wanted to reply to both with something savage. We looked at them together. Nazia has teased her like that for years and always ends with a plan, and Manjula half smiled reading it again. The second came from nobody she knew, in front of the whole class, clearly fishing for a reaction. We agreed she wouldn't answer it. We took screenshots with the dates showing, and before she left I emailed them to her class teacher at school and to her mother. The class teacher replied tonight: it will be taken up first thing Monday.

qa.q: Where was the anonymous message posted?
qa.a: It was posted under the class video, from an account with no photo.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling as she scrolled with her lips pressed tight?
qa.a: Manjula was hurt and angry, wanting to reply with something savage; the half smile at the first message suggests it was mainly the anonymous one that stung.

qa.q: Which protective moves did they choose, and why?
qa.a: They didn't answer the attack, saved screenshots with dates, and the tuition teacher emailed them to the class teacher and Manjula's mother so adults could act on evidence.

qa.q: What would change if Manjula had replied savagely to the anonymous account?
qa.a: It would give the poster the reaction they were fishing for in front of the whole class, and could make Manjula look like the attacker.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading one taunt as long-standing banter and another as an attack meant to provoke, then choosing not to answer and to save evidence.
